doc_summary: Buck Shlegeris explains AI control: assuming models are scheming and designing cheap, adversarially-tested protocols (auditing, resampling, untrusted monitoring, honeypots) to extract useful work anyway. Much of it concerns whether models can distinguish tests/honeypots from real deployment and what evidence is convincing.

items.claim: Prefers adversarial red-team evaluation that assumes the model is actively trying to evade the test over standard measurement of model values, because tests that ignore a strategic model's ability to hide give false reassurance.
items.quote: The way that I want people to think about checking for alignment is from this very control-ish perspective — where you really reason through, what would the model do if it was misaligned? And if it was misaligned, is there a strategy it could follow that would prevent it from being caught

items.claim: In a setup, do not rely on synthetic inputs that look like today's world (e.g. public 2025 libraries) when the model expects a future deployment, because staleness of the environment reveals it is a test; generate decoys during deployment or from real trajectories instead.
items.quote: Imagine you try to come up with a synthetic input for your untrusted monitor, and it's using a bunch of Python libraries that were all public in 2025. It can be like, "I must not be deep into the intelligence explosion

items.claim: A model needs a very strong likelihood-ratio signal to tell a honeypot from reality when it expects many honeypots, so any residual tell (style, idiom, passwords, context) is what makes a scenario eval-like.
items.quote: you start out with like a one is to a million prior on any particular attack that you see that you are being honeypotted. And so you have to somehow get a one-in-a-million likelihood ratio update towards this being real.

items.claim: In a setup, build scenarios by resampling or replaying real model-produced context (the exact same input string) instead of hand-writing fake continuations, because the model cannot distinguish a replayed prefix from the first time it saw it.
items.quote: whatever input you'd given to the AI before you sampled a previous action, that's just some string that you can produce by the same process that you produced it the first time. So there's actually no difficulty going back in time here.

items.claim: Distrusts using the untrusted model to generate or judge its own decoys, since it can embed steganographic collusion signals (e.g. an unidiomatic while loop) marking real versus fake.
items.quote: some of the attack strategies that Ryan Greenblatt came up with included "use a 'while loop' somewhere where a 'for loop' would have been more idiomatic as the signal that this is a real attack."

items.claim: Disguise the domain and purpose of tasks (strip context) so a model cannot selectively sandbag or behave differently based on knowing what the task is for.
items.quote: If you're able to give them questions while disguising what domain the question was from or why you were asking some subpart of the question, they can no longer follow this strategy.

items.claim: Prefers being conservative about model capabilities (assume it could coordinate on codes, attack at one-in-a-million rates) over assuming it can't, because safety arguments should not rest on unmeasured limits.
items.quote: I normally recommend being conservative about whether they can coordinate on a code, so I normally recommend assuming that the AIs did set up a code in advance.

items.claim: Prefers testing sequences of actions and resampling over judging a single action, because multi-step malign behavior is much easier to distinguish from benign than a single step.
items.quote: it's just generally a lot easier to tell the difference between five benign actions and five malign actions than to tell the difference between one benign action and one malign action.

items.claim: Treats a single clear incriminating example as strong evidence, but notes sceptics may dismiss it as rigged or aberrant, so convincingness depends on audience priors.
items.quote: I would at least claim that it was plausible that my competitor had rigged the training of their AI to make it so that it sometimes tried to escape — which would be very easy to do, and basically impossible to verify hadn't happened.

items.claim: Chooses what to test by measuring scheming-relevant capabilities directly (e.g. strategy datasets with/without chain of thought) rather than waiting for naturally occurring misbehavior.
items.quote: made a dataset of problems that are basically like a lot of the reasoning that we've been doing in this conversation. Like, "You're an AI, and they're like looking at you in such-and-such a situation, and they only get to look at you 1% of the time

items.claim: Wants research on scalable oversight explicitly assuming the AI is sabotaging the process, which has barely been done.
items.quote: Basically no research has been done explicitly on the topic of scalable oversight, except you're assuming that the AIs are trying to sabotage the whole process. I'm really excited for this research direction
